name: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
title: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
answer: Institutional knowledge graphs are structured representations of an organisation's people, projects, publications, datasets, equipment and their relationships, built so that questions spanning those entities can be answered from one connected source. In a research setting they typically cover outputs such as papers, claims, models, tools and glossary terms, and the links between them. The scope is deliberately narrower than the open web: it describes what the institution holds, funds, produces or stewards, and it stops at the boundary of that remit.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Institutional knowledge graphs are structured representations of an organisation's people, projects, publications, datasets, equipment and their relationships, built so that questions spanning those entities can be answered from one connected source. In a research setting they typically cover outputs such as papers, claims, models, tools and glossary terms, and the links between them. The scope is deliberately narrower than the open web: it describes what the institution holds, funds, produces or stewards, and it stops at the boundary of that remit.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These graphs run on a graph database or a triple store, with an ontology or schema that fixes the entity types and the allowed relations. Data arrives from source systems such as a repository, a CRUD system for projects, an HR feed and a publications database, usually through an extract, transform, load pipeline that reconciles identifiers. Persistent identifiers, including ORCID for people and DOI for outputs, do much of the matching work, and a search layer sits on top for query and retrieval.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work begins with ontology design, deciding which entities and relations matter and how granular the graph should be. Ingestion then maps each source record to that schema, resolves duplicates and merges records that describe the same thing. Curation follows, with subject specialists reviewing automated matches and filling gaps, and quality checks run against coverage, consistency and link validity. Queries and graph analytics then serve discovery, reporting and recommendation, and the graph is versioned so changes can be traced.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and provenance are the hard part, because a graph that joins records from several systems can expose personal data, unpublished findings or restricted datasets. Each node and edge needs a provenance trail back to its source record, and access rules need to be enforced at query time rather than only at ingestion. Licensing varies by source, so reuse terms must travel with the data, and corrections or retractions in a source system must propagate into the graph. Where the graph covers people, data protection obligations apply to the profiles it builds.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward graphs that update continuously rather than in periodic batches, and toward federation, where an institution's graph queries other institutions' graphs without centralising the data. Automated extraction from papers and datasets will keep expanding coverage, which raises the share of machine-generated edges needing review. Expect more emphasis on provenance standards and on interfaces that let non-specialists ask questions in natural language while the graph supplies the evidence.
